Confetti means isolated crosses or very small groups of one color surrounded by other shades. It is common in portraits, full coverage and photo conversions where tiny changes try to reproduce texture or shadow.

The key idea

Before committing many hours, test a small section with the actual fabric and thread. How to apply it

Before starting a dense area, locate appearances of the same symbol within a reasonable distance. Grouping a few nearby stitches reduces starts and finishes without forcing very long thread carries.

Work with measurable information: stitches, fabric count, strand number, usable width or color count. Those references prevent visual decisions from depending only on an enlarged preview. How materials change the result

The parking method can help when many colors interlock and each shade reappears soon. For occasional confetti, working small color groups may be simpler than managing dozens of parked threads.

View the stitching from the distance at which the finished piece will normally be seen. Cross stitch simplifies shape and color, and a solution that looks refined while zoomed in can become noise as an object. Common problems

Do not carry a strand a huge distance simply to avoid finishing it. Long carries waste floss, can show through pale fabric and create a back that is difficult to control.

Think about finishing before starting. Framing, washing, mounting on a textile or everyday use changes margins, materials and how important short secure thread paths become. When designing, review colors that appear in only a handful of stitches. Some define eyes, edges or tiny highlights; others are converter noise and can be merged into a neighboring shade without losing the image.
